title: Choose the map editor's visual world
question: Keep the letterpress worktable, choose an alternate, or ask for a fresh set.

options.label: Composing Table
options.lineage: letterpress composing stones and type drawers
options.thesis: Build the map like a printed proof: landscapes are sheets and pixel pieces are movable sorts.
options.viewport: A large painted forest map fills the center, framed by a narrow tool rail and an open drawer of crisp pixel characters.
options.risk: The printshop metaphor must remain functional and never make ordinary editing actions cryptic.

options.label: Scene & Cue Desk
options.lineage: theatre scene shops and cyclorama lighting desks
options.thesis: Treat the painted landscape as a stage and every pixel character as a cast member or prop.
options.viewport: The map is a brightly lit stage at center with a cast-and-props rail at left and scene controls along the bottom.
options.risk: Strong audience identification, but theatrical labels could obscure familiar file and layer concepts.
options.case: Nearly wins on audience identification; the composing table is clearer for grid placement and image export.

options.label: Grid Specimen
options.thesis: Let the battle grid become the visible armature for every control, label, and placed piece.
options.viewport: A monumental map occupies a strict modular grid while asset controls snap into the same visible cells.
options.risk: Excellent product clarity, but its clinical graphic language fights the painted-fantasy atmosphere.
options.case: Wins on grid clarity but loses decisively on the requested fantasy character of the finished map.

options.label: Teletext Bestiary
options.thesis: Make the asset library a numbered pixel bestiary with instant keyboard recall.
options.viewport: A dark 40-column frame surrounds the painted map while characters appear in bright indexed pixel compartments.
options.risk: Fuses poorly because its fixed black broadcast field competes with the painted landscape instead of supporting it.
options.case: Strongest pixel identity, but lower map clarity and weaker compatibility with painted backgrounds.

canonCard.label: Conventional map editor
canonCard.thesis: A familiar dark desktop editor with a toolbar, asset browser, central canvas, and properties panel.
canonCard.viewport: A standard three-panel editor surrounds the map with predictable Windows-style controls.
canonCard.risk: Immediately familiar but visually interchangeable with generic level editors.
